==Problem==

A number <imath>m</imath> is randomly selected from the set <imath>\{11,13,15,17,19\}</imath>, and a number <imath>n</imath> is randomly selected from <imath>\{1999,2000,2001,\ldots,2018\}</imath>. What is the probability that <imath>m^n</imath> has a units digit of <imath>1</imath>?

<imath>\textbf{(A) }   \frac{1}{5}   \qquad        \textbf{(B) }   \frac{1}{4}   \qquad    \textbf{(C) }   \frac{3}{10}   \qquad   \textbf{(D) } \frac{7}{20} \qquad  \textbf{(E) }   \frac{2}{5} </imath>

== Solution 1 ==
Since we only care about the units digit, our set <imath>\{11,13,15,17,19 \}</imath> can be turned into <imath>\{1,3,5,7,9 \}</imath>. Call this set <imath>A</imath> and call <imath>\{1999, 2000, 2001, \cdots , 2018 \}</imath> set <imath>B</imath>. Let's do casework on the element of <imath>A</imath> that we choose. Since <imath>1\cdot 1=1</imath>, any number from <imath>B</imath> can be paired with <imath>1</imath> to make <imath>1^n</imath> have a units digit of <imath>1</imath>. Therefore, the probability of this case happening is <imath>\frac{1}{5}</imath> since there is a <imath>\frac{1}{5}</imath> chance that the number <imath>1</imath> is selected from <imath>A</imath>. Let us consider the case where the number <imath>3</imath> is selected from <imath>A</imath>. Let's look at the unit digit when we repeatedly multiply the number <imath>3</imath> by itself:
<cmath>3\cdot 3=9</cmath>
<cmath>9\cdot 3=7</cmath> 
<cmath>7\cdot 3=1</cmath>
<cmath>1\cdot 3=3</cmath>
We see that the unit digit of <imath>3^x</imath>, for some integer <imath>x</imath>, will only be <imath>1</imath> when <imath>x</imath> is a multiple of <imath>4</imath>. Now, let's count how many numbers in <imath>B</imath> are divisible by <imath>4</imath>. This can be done by simply listing:
<cmath>2000,2004,2008,2012,2016.</cmath>
There are <imath>5</imath> numbers in <imath>B</imath> divisible by <imath>4</imath> out of the <imath>2018-1999+1=20</imath> total numbers. Therefore, the probability that <imath>3</imath> is picked from <imath>A</imath> and a number divisible by <imath>4</imath> is picked from <imath>B</imath> is <imath>\frac{1}{5}\cdot \frac{5}{20}=\frac{1}{20}.</imath>
Similarly, we can look at the repeating units digit for <imath>7</imath>:
<cmath>7\cdot 7=9</cmath>
<cmath>9\cdot 7=3</cmath>
<cmath>3\cdot 7=1</cmath>
<cmath>1\cdot 7=7</cmath>
We see that the unit digit of <imath>7^y</imath>, for some integer <imath>y</imath>, will only be <imath>1</imath> when <imath>y</imath> is a multiple of <imath>4</imath>. This is exactly the same conditions as our last case with <imath>3</imath> so the probability of this case is also <imath>\frac{1}{20}</imath>. 
Since <imath>5\cdot 5=25</imath> and <imath>25</imath> ends in <imath>5</imath>, the units digit of <imath>5^w</imath>, for some integer, <imath>w</imath> will always be <imath>5</imath>. Thus, the probability in this case is <imath>0</imath>.
The last case we need to consider is when the number <imath>9</imath> is chosen from <imath>A</imath>. This happens with probability <imath>\frac{1}{5}.</imath> We list out the repeating units digit for <imath>9</imath> as we have done for <imath>3</imath> and <imath>7</imath>:
<cmath>9\cdot 9=1</cmath>
<cmath>1\cdot 9=9</cmath>
We see that the units digit of <imath>9^z</imath>, for some integer <imath>z</imath>, is <imath>1</imath> only when <imath>z</imath> is an even number. From the <imath>20</imath> numbers in <imath>B</imath>, we see that exactly half of them are even. The probability in this case is <imath>\frac{1}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{10}.</imath>
Finally, we can add all of our probabilities together to get 
<cmath>\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{20}+\frac{1}{20}+\frac{1}{10}=\boxed{\textbf{(E)} ~\frac{2}{5}}.</cmath>

(I did not prove yet) 
{1999, 2000, 2001,..., 2018} is the same as {1,2,3,4,1,2,...,4}, which can be turned into {1,2,3,4}

== Solution 2 ==
Since only the units digit is relevant, we can turn the first set into <imath>\{1,3,5,7,9\}</imath>. Note that <imath>x^4 \equiv 1 \mod 10</imath> for all odd digits <imath>x</imath>, except for 5. Looking at the second set, we see that it is a set of all integers between 1999 and 2018. There are 20 members of this set, which means that, <imath>\mod 4</imath>, this set has 5 values which correspond to <imath>\{0,1,2,3\}</imath>, making the probability equal for all of them. Next, check the values for which it is equal to <imath>1 \mod 10</imath>. There are <imath>4+1+0+1+2=8</imath> values for which it is equal to 1, remembering that <imath>5^{4n} \equiv 1 \mod 10</imath> only if <imath>n=0</imath>, which it is not. There are 20 values in total, and simplifying <imath>\frac{8}{20}</imath> gives us <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(E)} ~\frac{2}{5}}</imath>.

==Solution 3==
By Euler's Theorem, we have that <imath>a^{4} \equiv 1 \pmod {10}</imath>, if <imath>\gcd(a,10)=1</imath>. 
Hence <imath>m=11,13,17,19</imath>, <imath>n=2000,2004,2008,2012,2016</imath> work. 

Also note that <imath>11^{\text{any positive integer}}\equiv 1 \pmod {10}</imath> because <imath>11^b=(10+1)^b=10^b+10^{b-1}1+...+10(1)+1</imath>, and the latter <imath>\pmod {10}</imath> is clearly <imath>1</imath>. So <imath>m=11</imath>, <imath>n=1999,2001,2002,2003,2005,...,2018</imath> work (not counting multiples of 4 as we would be double counting if we did). 

We can also note that <imath>19^{2a}\equiv 1 \pmod {10}</imath> because <imath>19^{2a}=361^{a}</imath>, and by the same logic as why <imath>11^{\text{any positive integer}}\equiv 1 \pmod {10}</imath>, we are done. Hence <imath>m=19</imath>, and <imath>n=2002, 2006, 2010, 2014, 2018</imath> work (not counting any of the aforementioned cases as that would be double counting). 

We cannot make any more observations that add more <imath>m^n</imath> with unit digit <imath>1</imath>, hence the number of <imath>m^n</imath> that have units digit one is <imath>4\cdot 5+1\cdot 15+1\cdot 5=40</imath>. And the total number of combinations of an element of the set of all <imath>m</imath> and an element of the set of all <imath>n</imath> is <imath>5\cdot 20=100</imath>. Hence the desired probability is <imath>\frac{40}{100}=\frac{2}{5}</imath>, which is answer choice <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(E)} ~\frac{2}{5}}</imath>. 
~vsamc

==Solution 4 (Easy)==
When a number's unit's digit is <imath>1</imath>, then any power to this number will also end in <imath>1</imath> (since <imath>1^{n}</imath> for any <imath>n</imath> is always <imath>1</imath>), so we have <imath>20</imath> choices for <imath>11</imath>.

When a number's unit's digit is <imath>3</imath>, then <imath>3^{4n}</imath> for any <imath>n</imath> will produce a number ending with 1. So, <imath>20 \div 4 = 5</imath> choices for <imath>13</imath>.

<imath>5^{n}</imath> always ends in 5, so there are <imath>0</imath> possibilities for <imath>15</imath>. 

When a number's unit's digit is <imath>7</imath>, then this is also the same thing with <imath>3</imath>, so we have <imath>5</imath> choices.

When a number's unit's digit is <imath>9</imath>, then <imath>9^{2n}</imath> will produce a number ending in <imath>1</imath>, so we have <imath>20 \div 2 = 10</imath> possibilities. 

Hence, we have a total of <imath>5 \cdot 20 = 100</imath> ways, so the probability is <imath>\frac{20+5+0+5+10}{100} = \frac {40}{100} = \boxed{\textbf{(E)} ~\frac{2}{5}}</imath>. 

~MrThinker

==Solution 5==
Since exponents have the properties to loop between 4 unit digits, by filtering through the first 5 numbers, we can see that only <imath>11, 13, 17</imath> and <imath>19</imath> are left. Now we need to get the <imath>mod4</imath> of  all the exponents, and by doing so we get this from the modulo:
<cmath>{3, 0, 1, 2, 3 \cdot \cdot \cdot 2}</cmath>
Now we start going through all numbers:
all <imath>11</imath>'s result in a unit digit of 1;
For <imath>13 and 17</imath>, only when the remainder is 0 is when the unit digit is 1; 
Lastly, for 19, when the remainder is equaled to 0,2 is when the unit digit equals to 1;
By adding all of them up and dividing them by 100:
<cmath>20+5+5+10 = 40</cmath>
and <imath>\frac {40}{100} = \boxed{\textbf{(E)} ~\frac{2}{5}}</imath>. 

~Alomonde~
